Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

forget verb

also forget to, I forgot, forgotten, don’t forget, slip one’s mind, forget about it!, forget it!, put it out of your mind, it slipped my mind, it slipped my mind to, it has slipped my mind

classical

Cic. Sen. 21: oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset
Petr. 49.1: sē oblītum esse exinterāre
Traupman 318

oblīvīscor, oblīvīscī, oblītus sum

Lewis & Short: the person forgotten in the genitive, a thing in the genitive or the accusative; less often an infinitive, forget to (Petr. 49.1), or a question, forget where or what (Cic. Sen. 21). “Don’t forget” is nōlī oblīvīscī (Traupman 163), or mementō with an infinitive (see remember).

Other words

  • excidō, excidere, excidī — slip from the memory: excidit mihi, it has slipped my mind

    verb, third conjugation, intransitive: what is forgotten is the subject, the person in the dative · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 6.1.7: mihi nōn excidisse illud; Liv. 29.19.12: excidisse dē memoriā; M-O s.v. forget; Traupman 107: it has slipped my mind, memoriā excidit

    Literally “fall out”: also ex animō or dē memoriā excidere (Lewis & Short).

  • dēdiscō, dēdiscere, dēdidicī — unlearn, forget what one has learned

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Am. 688: quī quod didicit id dēdiscit

    Lewis & Short: rare, but classical.

  • fugit mē (+ inf.) — it slipped my mind (to do), I forgot (to)

    impersonal: the thing forgotten is the subject or an infinitive, the person in the accusative · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 7.18.3: dē Dionȳsiō, fugit mē ad tē anteā scrībere (Lewis & Short s.v. fugiō); Traupman 104: it slipped my mind to write to you, fūgit mē ad tē scrībere

    Literally “it escaped me”. Traupman prints the perfect, fūgit; Cicero’s present fugit mē serves for what one has just realised one forgot. With a clause, tē nōn fugit is “you are well aware”.

Examples

  • sē oblītum esse exinterāre. — quid, oblītus?

    he said he had forgotten to gut it. — What, forgotten?Petr. 49.1

  • nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset

    and I never heard of an old man who forgot where he had buried his treasureCic. Sen. 21

  • sed plānē tē intellegere voluī mihi nōn excidisse illud quod tū ad mē quibusdam litterīs scrīpsissēs

    but I wanted you to see quite clearly that I had not forgotten what you once wrote to me in a letterCic. Att. 6.1.7

  • Ējice id ex animō!

    Forget about it!Traupman 98

See also remember, memory, learn by heart.
